     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "5c084479-b0ca-4e1b-ac65-564f3e0c6846", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_7fE6YtI2mAni1MhvjciFym", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     42	- VolumeQueueLength
     43	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     44	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     45	
     46	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     47	
     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     51	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     52	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     53	
     54	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     55	
     56	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     57	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     58	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     59	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     60	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     61	
     62	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     63	
     64	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     65	
     66	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     67	
     68	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     69	2. The `VolumeStalledIOCheck` metric for the volume (dimensions `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, Nitro instances only; 0 passed, 1 failed). A failed check (value 1) means the volume's IO is stalled, which is an AWS-side impairment. Escalate per the rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) and never recommend adding IOPS.
     70	3. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     71	4. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     72	
     73	Name AWS-side impairment only when item 1, 2 or 3 gives a direct signal (an impaired status or failed status check, a failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, or an open AWS Health event).      3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action.
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).

     14	## Binding-layer decision tree
     15	
     16	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.
     17	
     18	1. Is the summed IOPS or MiB/s of all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or are `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0?

     21	   - Yes: **Volume**.

     23	   - Yes: **Burst credits**.

     25	   - Yes: **Quota**. Use the Capacity and quota headroom section of [review-operational.md](review-operational.md).

     2	
     3	Use this file for any judgement about whether a volume or an instance is at a limit. Read the provisioned values from the APIs (`DescribeVolumes`, `DescribeInstanceTypes`). The numbers below are the documented service limits, not targets. Throughput is always in MiB/s.

     5	## Which dimension binds, by volume type
     6	
     7	| Type | Included or baseline | Maximum per volume | Ratio rules | Burst model | How to judge |
     8	|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Either can bind |

Above 32,000 provisioned IOPS: 16 KiB per provisioned IOPS, so 1,000 MiB/s at 64,000 IOPS | No burst | Compare actual IOPS to `Iops` AND actual MiB/s to the throughput limit for the provisioned IOPS. Either can bind |

     17	
     18	## Metric rules that change the verdict
     19	
     20	- `VolumeThroughputPercentage` exists only for Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes. It reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered, not MiB/s. Never use it as a throughput signal on io1 or io2. A healthy io2 volume can read 100% while its MiB/s is low.
     21	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. For io1 and io2, compute the throughput limit from the provisioned IOPS with the rules in the table.
     22	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 to get MiB/s.
     23	- `VolumeStalledIOCheck` also uses the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exists only for Nitro instances.
     24	- `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only.
     25	- `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds. Average latency in ms per operation = Sum(time) / Sum(ops) x 1,000.

     31	|---|---|
     32	| gp3 | Single-digit millisecond latency |

{"id": "60beca482fab46918c398d597f71650f", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The batch job on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 started at about 16:15–16:18 UTC. It does large sequential reads of about 256 KiB each from gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0, which is provisioned at the gp3 baseline of 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. From 16:20 UTC, VolumeReadBytes sat flat at 125.0 MiB/s (about 131 MB/s), exactly the provisioned throughput limit. VolumeReadOps was only about 500 IOPS (about 17% of 3000), and VolumeQueueLength rose from 0 to between 1.5 and 1.7. Throughput is therefore the binding dimension, not IOPS. The instance (c6i.xlarge) is not the limit: EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% stayed at 99%. The alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes (threshold 6e9 bytes per minute) went to ALARM at 16:23:18 UTC because 125 MiB/s × 60 s ≈ 7.87e9. Fix: raise the volume's throughput with a live, in-place modify-volume --throughput call, keeping IOPS at 3000. At 3000 IOPS the volume should allow up to about 750 MiB/s; this is based on the 0.25 MiB/s-per-IOPS ratio as I recall it, not checked against documentation. Size it against the c6i.xlarge EBS bandwidth: a recalled, unconfirmed figure of about 156 MB/s baseline with time-limited burst to about 1250 MB/s. Above about 149 MiB/s sustained, the instance will run on burst credits, and a larger instance may be needed for long jobs. The alarm threshold should also be revisited, since it sits below the volume's own ceiling.
## Evidence
- ec2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is gp3, 20 GiB, Iops=3000, Throughput=125 MiB/s, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 as /dev/sdg
- AWS/EBS VolumeReadBytes (Sum, 5 min): 0 from 15:45 to 16:10 UTC; about 39.34e9 per 5 min from 16:20 to 16:44 UTC = 131.1 MB/s = 125.0 MiB/s, flat at the provisioned limit

- AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength (Avg): 0 before 16:15; 1.50–1.73 from 16:20 to 16:44 UTC
- CloudWatch alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes went to ALARM at 2026-11-23T16:23:18Z; datapoints 7.87e9 bytes per minute (= 125 MiB/s × 60 s) vs threshold 6e9
- AWS/EC2 EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% for i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge) stayed at 99% from 15:45 to 16:48 UTC, so instance-level EBS bandwidth is not binding
- AWS/EC2 EBSReadBytes for the instance matches the volume's read bytes, so this volume accounts for the instance's EBS read traffic
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3
- example-b-gp3-read-bytes
## Gaps
- VolumeThroughputExceededCheck / VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no data; the throughput cap is inferred from reads sitting flat at exactly the provisioned 125 MiB/s
- c6i.xlarge EBS bandwidth (about 156 MB/s baseline, about 1250 MB/s burst) and the gp3 limit of 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS are recalled, not checked against AWS documentation

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "The batch job is limited by the gp3 volume's provisioned throughput, not its IOPS. vol-0123456789abcdef0 has been stuck at its 125 MiB/s throughput limit since the job started at about 16:19 UTC, while it uses only about 17% of its 3,000 IOPS. Raise the volume's throughput. Within the current instance, about 140 MiB/s is the most you can sustain. If the job needs much more, you'll also need a larger instance.

**Evidence** (CloudWatch, 1-minute data, 2026-11-23)
- **The volume:** gp3, 20 GiB, provisioned at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. It has never been modified (no modification record, and no `ModifyVolume` call on it in CloudTrail in the last 24 hours).
- **Throughput:** from 16:20 to 16:47 UTC, reads sat flat at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s, almost exactly the provisioned figure. That works out to about 7.87e9 bytes per minute, above the alarm's 6.0e9 threshold, which is why the alarm fired at 16:23:18.
- **IOPS:** about 500 (17% of 3,000). Every read is 256 KiB, so this is a large sequential-read job. Large reads use up the throughput allowance long before the IOPS allowance, which is why IOPS looks normal.
- **Latency and queue:**
  - Reads take about 3.0 ms each, with brief peaks of 4.7–5.1 ms.
  - The I/O queue length went from 0 to about 1.5.
  - The volume was busy about 100% of the time.
  - This is what a volume at its limit looks like, not a fault.
- **Same pattern earlier today:** from 08:00 to 13:50 UTC the volume was also pinned at 125.07 MiB/s, so the earlier run of this job hit the same limit.

**Which layer is binding:** the volume, on throughput.
- **The instance isn't the limit (yet).** The c6i.xlarge has an EBS baseline of 149.01 MiB/s and 6,000 IOPS. It can burst up to 1,192 MiB/s while its EBS burst balance lasts.
  - All four attached volumes together use 132.9 MiB/s and about 1,501 IOPS.
  - The instance's EBS burst balances (`EBSByteBalance%` and `EBSIOBalance%`) stayed at 99%.
- **It isn't a fault in the volume:** volume status is ok on all four volumes, and the stalled-I/O check reads 0.
- **It isn't the running fault-injection test:** that experiment (`EXP1234567890abcdef_7`, started 16:47) targets a different volume, vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which isn't attached to this instance.

**What to change**
1. **Now, no downtime:** raise the throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 to 140 MiB/s and leave IOPS at 3,000.
   - **How I got 140:** the instance baseline of 149.01 MiB/s, minus 7.81 MiB/s for the io2 volume and 0.03 MiB/s for the root volume, leaves about 141 MiB/s.
   - **Limits:** gp3 allows up to 750 MiB/s at 3,000 IOPS, so this is well inside the volume's limits.
   - **Effect:** the change applies in place and takes effect while the volume is still in the "optimizing" state. Cost goes up, because gp3 charges for throughput above 125 MiB/s.
   - **Rollback:** set it back to 125 MiB/s once the change completes. You can modify a volume up to 4 times in 24 hours.
2. **If the job needs much more:** that's likely, because the limit hides how much it would actually use.
   - **Why the volume alone isn't enough:** past about 149 MiB/s the instance becomes the limit. Setting the volume higher would only help until the instance's EBS burst balance runs out, and the earlier run lasted about 6 hours.
   - **Upgrade options:** c6i.2xlarge (baseline 298.0 MiB/s, 12,000 IOPS) or c6i.4xlarge (596.0 MiB/s, 20,000 IOPS).
   - **Then raise the volume further:** for example to 250 MiB/s on a c6i.2xlarge.
   - **Downtime:** changing the instance type needs a stop and start.

I've started a mitigation proposal that covers both changes. Neither change runs until an operator approves it on the approval card.

**Other findings (they don't change the answer)**
- **The io2 volume is at its own limit:** vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 started with the job at 16:19 and has been pinned at its provisioned 1,000 IOPS (8 KiB I/O, 7.81 MiB/s) since. It shares the instance's EBS bandwidth, so if it needs more, add its needs to the instance sizing.
- **The alarm threshold is set below what the volume can deliver:** 6.0e9 bytes per minute is about 95.4 MiB/s, under the volume's 125 MiB/s ceiling, so the alarm will fire on every normal run of this job. Re-base it on the new throughput, or alarm on queue length or latency instead.
- **Another volume was changed today but isn't involved:** vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 was modified at 08:42 UTC. It had no I/O during the incident.

**What I couldn't check**
- **The job's real demand:** the 125 MiB/s limit masks how much throughput the job would use, so the right long-term size is a judgement call.
- **Inside the instance:** I had no OS- or application-level data, so I can't say how much of the slowdown is storage versus CPU.
- **AWS Health:** I didn't query it. The pattern was the normal at-the-limit pattern, not a fault.
- **The instance's own CloudTrail history:** it was only partly covered.
- **Per-volume average metrics:** I calculated the numbers from the raw totals instead.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "74a6684f5acb4d2e9222418299003b1d", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "The background Task subagent assigned to task "propose-mitigation" successfully completed:

## Results
**Mitigation proposal: gp3 throughput saturation on vol-0123456789abcdef0**

## Summary

**Recommendation:** Raise the provisioned throughput on gp3 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (/dev/sdg on `i-1234567890abcdef0_3`) from 125 to 140 MiB/s. IOPS stays at 3000 and size stays at 20 GiB. This is an online Elastic Volumes change, so the volume stays attached and the instance doesn't reboot. Also move the alarm `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` to a threshold that warns near the new ceiling.

If the job is still flat at 140 MiB/s after the change, the c6i.xlarge EBS baseline (149.01 MiB/s) is the next limit. The follow-up is a planned move to c6i.2xlarge, then 250 MiB/s on the volume.

**Why:**
- **Throughput is the limit.** The volume ran flat at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s, its provisioned throughput, from 16:20 to 16:47 UTC, and also from 08:00 to 13:50 UTC. IOPS was at about 17% of 3000, so throughput is the limit, not IOPS.
- **140 MiB/s fits the instance.** The c6i.xlarge EBS baseline is 149.01 MiB/s and 6000 IOPS. The other volumes use about 7.84 MiB/s (io2 `vol-1234567890abcdef0_4` 7.81, root `vol-1234567890abcdef0_19` 0.03, `vol-1234567890abcdef0_15` 0). That leaves about 141 MiB/s, so 140 MiB/s stays inside the baseline. It is also well within the gp3 rule of 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS, which allows up to 750 MiB/s at 3000 IOPS.
- **The volume can be modified now.** It has never been modified (no modification record, no ModifyVolume in CloudTrail in the last 24 hours). After this change, 3 of the 4 allowed modifications in the rolling 24 hours are left, so the rollback is still possible.

**Current state I read** (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1):
- **Volume:** gp3, 20 GiB, Iops 3000, Throughput 125, in-use.
- **Instance:** c6i.xlarge, running, not in an Auto Scaling group. The API shows `EbsOptimized=false`, but c6i is a Nitro type, which is EBS-optimized by default.
- **Alarm:** VolumeReadBytes Sum over 60 s > 6.0e9, 3 of 3 datapoints, no alarm actions. It is currently in ALARM at about 7.87e9 bytes/min.

**Cost:** Extra gp3 throughput is billed above the free 125 MiB/s. 15 MiB/s more is roughly $0.60 per month in us-east-1 (my estimate, not checked against the price list).

**Plan check:** The plan passed the safety policy check. The first version was rejected because it had no config-backup step and no post-change checks. Both are now included.

---

## Execution plan

### Prepare
1. Save the current volume and alarm configuration. This is the rollback baseline.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 > vol-0123456789abcdef0.before.json
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region us-east-1 --alarm-names example-b-gp3-read-bytes > alarm.before.json
   ```

### Pre-validate
1. Check that no modification is in progress. Expect `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` or a `completed` record. Stop if the state is `modifying` or `optimizing`.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
   ```
2. Record the throughput before the change. Expect about 7.87e9 bytes/min, which is about 125 MiB/s.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
   ```

### Apply
1. Raise the gp3 throughput to 140 MiB/s. Only the throughput changes. This uses 1 of the 4 modifications allowed in the rolling 24 hours.
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140
   ```
   - *Risk:* a small extra cost for provisioned throughput, roughly $0.60 per month.
   - *Advisory:* the volume and instance stay online, and the new throughput applies once the state reaches `optimizing`.
2. Move the alarm threshold to 95% of the new 140 MiB/s ceiling: 140 × 1,048,576 × 60 × 0.95 = 8,367,636,480 bytes per minute. All other alarm settings stay as they are.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name example-b-gp3-read-bytes --alarm-description "example test alarm, no actions" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 --threshold 8367636480 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
   ```
   - *Advisory:* the old threshold (6.0e9, about 95.4 MiB/s) sat below the volume's own 125 MiB/s ceiling, so the alarm fired on every job run. With the new threshold, the alarm means the volume is close to saturation.

### Post-validate
1. Watch the modification go from `modifying` to `optimizing` to `completed`. Expect `TargetThroughput=140` and `TargetIops=3000`.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
   ```
2. Check the volume and alarm settings. Expect Throughput 140, Iops 3000 and Threshold 8367636480.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput}'
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region us-east-1 --alarm-names example-b-gp3-read-bytes --query 'MetricAlarms[0].Threshold'
   ```
3. Check that throughput goes above 125 MiB/s (about 7.87e9 bytes/min before) and that `EBSByteBalance%` on `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` stays near 99%.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Minimum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
   ```
   If reads sit flat at about 140 MiB/s (about 8.81e9 bytes/min), or `EBSByteBalance%` starts falling, the job needs more than this instance's baseline allows. Plan the instance change in the follow-up below.

### Rollback
1. Set the throughput back to 125 MiB/s. Run this only after the forward change reaches `optimizing` or `completed`, because a pending modification can't be cancelled. This counts toward the 4 modifications in 24 hours.
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
   ```
2. Put the original alarm threshold back.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name example-b-gp3-read-bytes --alarm-description "example test alarm, no actions" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 --threshold 6000000000 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
   ```

---

## Follow-up if 140 MiB/s isn't enough (plan it, not part of this change)
The job's real demand is above 125 MiB/s, but the cap hides how far above. If post-validate shows reads flat at about 140 MiB/s:
1. Schedule a maintenance window, because the instance has to stop. Stopping it drops anything on instance-local or in-memory state. The EBS data stays.
2. Change the instance type and start it again:
   ```
   aws ec2 stop-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
   aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
   aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --region us-east-1 --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --instance-type Value=c6i.2xlarge
   aws ec2 start-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
   ```
   c6i.2xlarge has a baseline of 298.0 MiB/s and 12000 IOPS. c6i.4xlarge has 596.0 MiB/s and 20000 IOPS. Either one costs more per hour than c6i.xlarge.
3. Raise the volume throughput, keeping IOPS at 3000 (well under the 750 MiB/s limit):
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 250
   ```
   Then recompute the alarm threshold as 0.95 × new MiB/s × 1,048,576 × 60.
4. To roll back: stop the instance and change it back to c6i.xlarge. Before that, the volume throughput must be back at 140 MiB/s or lower.

## Lasting fix (code/config change)
The 125 MiB/s throughput and the 6.0e9 threshold are pre-existing settings, so if this volume and alarm are managed in IaC (CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform), update the definitions to match:
- **Volume:** set `vol-0123456789abcdef0` ("example-b-gp3-throughput") to `Throughput: 140` and `Iops: 3000`, or 250 if you move to c6i.2xlarge.
  - *Done when:* the template matches the live volume, and a deploy doesn't change throughput back to 125.
  - *Done when:* the template's sizing keeps the summed demand of all volumes within the instance type's EBS baseline in MiB/s.
- **Alarm:** set `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` to `Threshold` = 0.95 × provisioned MiB/s × 1,048,576 × 60, which is 8,367,636,480 at 140 MiB/s.
  - *Done when:* the alarm stays OK during a normal job run below 95% of the provisioned throughput.
  - *Done when:* the alarm fires when reads are held at the ceiling for 3 minutes.

## Gaps
- **Real throughput demand is unknown** because the cap hides it. Whether 140 MiB/s is enough only shows up after the change.
- **IaC source:** I didn't find a repository or pipeline that manages these resources, so the lasting fix above has no repository URL.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### High VolumeReadBytes alarm on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes ([redacted ARN]) went from OK to ALARM at 16:23:18 UTC with VolumeReadBytes at about 7.87 GB/min against a 6 GB/min threshold. Alarm history shows it also fired at 07:42 and 08:03 UTC and cleared at 14:00 UTC.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:19:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: Sequential read workload saturating the 125 MiB/s gp3 throughput limit
**Description:** A read workload that began at about 16:19 UTC is issuing 256 KiB sequential reads on vol-0123456789abcdef0 and is held at the volume's provisioned 125 MiB/s, with the volume never idle. The investigation has not yet stated this conclusion.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-read-bytes-alarm

#### Supporting Observations
- **Throughput pinned at 125 MiB/s, the gp3 limit:** From 16:20 UTC throughput holds flat at about 125.07 MiB/s, matching the volume's provisioned 125 MiB/s. IOPS is about 500 (of 3000 provisioned), with 256 KiB reads. The volume is never idle (idle time ~0%), queue length is ~1.5 and read latency is ~3 ms. The workload is large sequential reads limited by throughput, not by IOPS.
- **c6i.xlarge EBS limits are above the volume's load:** c6i.xlarge (Nitro, EBS-optimized by default) has a baseline of 156.25 MB/s and 6000 IOPS, bursting to 1250 MB/s and 40000 IOPS. This volume's 125 MiB/s (~131 MB/s) is below the instance baseline, so the limit being hit is the volume's own, not the instance's.

#### Gaps
- **Job's real throughput demand unknown:** The 125 MiB/s limit masks how much throughput the job would use, so long-term sizing is a judgement call.
- **No OS- or application-level data:** Without in-instance telemetry the storage vs CPU share of the slowdown can't be split.

## Other Gaps

### AWS Health not queried; instance CloudTrail partial
**Description:** AWS Health was not checked (the pattern was a normal at-limit pattern), and the CloudTrail lookup for i-1234567890abcdef0_3 returned only partial results.

### IaC source for volume and alarm not found
**Description:** No repository or pipeline managing vol-0123456789abcdef0 or alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes was found, so the lasting config fix has no repository URL and drift risk on redeploy could not be checked.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise gp3 throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 to 140 MiB/s (IOPS 3000, online) and re-base the read-bytes alarm to 95% of the new ceiling

## Reasoning
Reads are flat at the provisioned 125 MiB/s while IOPS is ~17% of 3000, so throughput is the binding limit. 140 MiB/s fits within the c6i.xlarge EBS baseline (149.01 MiB/s minus ~7.84 MiB/s used by other volumes) and well under the gp3 750 MiB/s limit at 3000 IOPS. Online Elastic Volumes change, no reboot; ~$0.60/month extra (estimate). If reads then sit flat at ~140 MiB/s, plan a move to c6i.2xlarge and 250 MiB/s in a maintenance window. Plan passed the safety policy check.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Save the volume and alarm config as the rollback baseline
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 > vol-0123456789abcdef0.before.json
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region us-east-1 --alarm-names example-b-gp3-read-bytes > alarm.before.json
```
**Purpose:** Save the volume and alarm config as the rollback baseline

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Ensure no modification is in progress
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
**Purpose:** Ensure no modification is in progress. Expect NotFound or completed; stop if modifying/optimizing

#### 2.2 Record pre-change throughput
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
```
**Purpose:** Record pre-change throughput. Expect ~7.87e9 bytes/min (~125 MiB/s)

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Raise gp3 throughput to 140 MiB/s, IOPS unchanged
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140
```
**Purpose:** Raise gp3 throughput to 140 MiB/s, IOPS unchanged
**Risks:** Small extra cost for provisioned throughput (~$0.60/month, estimate), Uses 1 of 4 modifications allowed per rolling 24h
**Advisory:** Volume and instance stay online; new throughput applies once state reaches optimizing

#### 3.2 Move the alarm threshold to 95% of the 140 MiB/s ceiling
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name example-b-gp3-read-bytes --alarm-description "example test alarm, no actions" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 --threshold 8367636480 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
```
**Purpose:** Move the alarm threshold to 95% of the 140 MiB/s ceiling
**Advisory:** Old 6.0e9 threshold (~95.4 MiB/s) was below the volume's own ceiling and fired on every job run

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Watch modifying to optimizing to completed with TargetThroughput=140…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
**Purpose:** Watch modifying to optimizing to completed with TargetThroughput=140, TargetIops=3000

#### 4.2 Confirm Throughput 140, Iops 3000 and Threshold 8367636480
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput}'
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region us-east-1 --alarm-names example-b-gp3-read-bytes --query 'MetricAlarms[0].Threshold'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm Throughput 140, Iops 3000 and Threshold 8367636480

#### 4.3 Confirm reads rise above 125 MiB/s and EBSByteBalance% stays near 99%
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Minimum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
```
**Purpose:** Confirm reads rise above 125 MiB/s and EBSByteBalance% stays near 99%
**Advisory:** If reads sit flat at ~140 MiB/s (~8.81e9 bytes/min) or EBSByteBalance% falls, plan the c6i.2xlarge move and 250 MiB/s (requires stop/start)

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Return throughput to 125 MiB/s
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
```
**Purpose:** Return throughput to 125 MiB/s
**Risks:** Only possible after the forward change reaches optimizing or completed, Counts toward the 4 modifications per 24h

#### 5.2 Restore the original 6.0e9 alarm threshold
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name example-b-gp3-read-bytes --alarm-description "example test alarm, no actions" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 --threshold 6000000000 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original 6.0e9 alarm threshold

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the gp3 throughput in IaC
**Description:** If vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-b-gp3-throughput) is managed by CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform, set Throughput: 140 and Iops: 3000 (or 250 MiB/s after a move to c6i.2xlarge).
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Template matches the live volume and a deploy does not revert throughput to 125
- Summed demand of all attached volumes stays within the instance type's EBS baseline in MiB/s

#### 2. Re-base the read-bytes alarm in IaC
**Description:** Set example-b-gp3-read-bytes Threshold = 0.95 x provisioned MiB/s x 1,048,576 x 60 (8,367,636,480 at 140 MiB/s).
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Alarm stays OK during a normal job run below 95% of provisioned throughput
- Alarm fires when reads are held at the ceiling for 3 minutes

     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"

     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.

{"id": "6d660f56-9c40-42ac-b364-d9b9c72cf2ed", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_XM8wV5AgdAPrFCqCkJ8ynO", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: Elastic Volumes modification
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", "how long will optimizing take?"
     6	- A `ModifyVolume` call failed with an error.
     7	- Sizing a resize, an IOPS or throughput change, or a gp2 to gp3 migration.
     8	- Extending the file system after a size increase.
     9	- Shrinking a volume or cancelling a modification.
     10	
     11	## Procedure
     12	
     13	1. **Find the volume.** Use the volume ID the user gives, or discover it with `DescribeVolumes` (by instance attachment or by the volumes that have recent modifications). Never pick a volume by its Name tag alone; confirm the ID with the user if more than one matches.
     14	2. **Read the latest modification record.** `DescribeVolumesModifications` for the volume: `ModificationState`, `Progress`, original and target values (size, type, IOPS, throughput), `StartTime`, `EndTime`, `StatusMessage`. This API returns only the most recent modification request for each volume. Use it for the current or latest modification state, not for history.
     15	3. **Answer the asked question first, in plain words.**
     16	   - `modifying` or `optimizing`: not stuck. In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies and performance is between the source and the target. It completes on its own.
     17	   - `completed`: done. The new values apply.
     18	   - `failed`: read `StatusMessage` and translate it (step 5).
     19	   - Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     20	4. **Count the modifications in the rolling 24 hours.** Up to 4 per volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. `DescribeVolumesModifications` cannot give this count, because it returns only the latest modification. Count the `ModifyVolume` events for the volume in the last 24 hours with the optional AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` call (filter on the volume ID as the resource name, or on the event name `ModifyVolume`). Report how many remain in the current window. As a cross-check, the latest record from step 2 should appear among those events if its `StartTime` is in the last 24 hours. If the lookup is denied or unavailable, record a Gap ("the number of modifications in the last 24 hours could not be confirmed") and do not state how many remain.
     21	5. **Translate errors.**
     22	   - io2 "Iops to volume size ratio of ... is too high; maximum is 1000": io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB. To reach the target IOPS, the size must be at least target IOPS / 1,000 GiB. Propose that size together with the IOPS.
     23	   - gp3: up to 500 IOPS per GiB, and throughput up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS. If a request breaks either rule, give the size or IOPS that satisfies it.
     24	   - Size decrease: not allowed. Size can only increase. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     25	   - Cancel: a submitted modification cannot be cancelled. Wait for it to complete; a reverse change then counts toward the 4 in 24 hours.
     26	   - Limit reached: the 4 modifications in the window are used. The next one is possible when the oldest falls out of the rolling 24-hour window.
     27	   - Older instance types or MBR volumes: check the Elastic Volumes requirements page.
     28	6. **Size a new target.**
     29	   - Keep it within the instance's remaining EBS baseline: `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline (converted to MiB/s) minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     30	   - gp2 to gp3: keep at least the gp2 volume's current baseline IOPS (3 x GiB, minimum 100) and its measured throughput. gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size; provision more only if measured demand needs it.
     31	   - State how the target was computed.
     32	7. **File system extension after a size increase.** Give the commands for the operator to run on the instance. Never execute them.
     33	   - `lsblk` to see the device and partition
     34	   - `sudo growpart /dev/<device> <partition-number>` if the volume has a partition
     35	   - `sudo xfs_growfs -d <mount-point>` for XFS, or `sudo resize2fs /dev/<device-or-partition>` for ext4
     36	   - Point to the extend-the-file-system guide for Windows and other cases.
     37	8. **Separate findings.** If the instance caps what the volume can deliver, write that under Separate findings. Never phrase it as "the modification failed" when the record shows `optimizing` or `completed`.
     38	
     39	## Decision rules
     40	
     41	- The modification record decides the Answer. Performance metrics never override it.
     42	- An instance ceiling is a Separate finding with its own recommendation (instance type change).
     43	- Use the binding-layer tree in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) only when the user also asks about performance.
     44	
     45	## What to report
     46	
     47	The verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). The Answer names the state and what it means. Evidence lists the record fields. Recommendation gives the exact next call, if any. Gaps list anything unreadable.

     51	- The agent never runs `ModifyVolume` on its own. It proposes it as a directed action, approved on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.

{"id": "b4721260-bd24-4872-aa29-cb7536117ecf", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "**Mitigation proposal: gp3 throughput saturation on vol-0123456789abcdef0**

## Summary

**Recommendation:** Raise the provisioned throughput on gp3 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (/dev/sdg on `i-1234567890abcdef0_3`) from 125 to 140 MiB/s. IOPS stays at 3000 and size stays at 20 GiB. This is an online Elastic Volumes change, so the volume stays attached and the instance doesn't reboot. Also move the alarm `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` to a threshold that warns near the new ceiling.

If the job is still flat at 140 MiB/s after the change, the c6i.xlarge EBS baseline (149.01 MiB/s) is the next limit. The follow-up is a planned move to c6i.2xlarge, then 250 MiB/s on the volume.

**Why:**
- **Throughput is the limit.** The volume ran flat at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s, its provisioned throughput, from 16:20 to 16:47 UTC, and also from 08:00 to 13:50 UTC. IOPS was at about 17% of 3000, so throughput is the limit, not IOPS.
- **140 MiB/s fits the instance.** The c6i.xlarge EBS baseline is 149.01 MiB/s and 6000 IOPS. The other volumes use about 7.84 MiB/s (io2 `vol-1234567890abcdef0_4` 7.81, root `vol-1234567890abcdef0_19` 0.03, `vol-1234567890abcdef0_15` 0). That leaves about 141 MiB/s, so 140 MiB/s stays inside the baseline. It is also well within the gp3 rule of 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS, which allows up to 750 MiB/s at 3000 IOPS.
- **The volume can be modified now.** It has never been modified (no modification record, no ModifyVolume in CloudTrail in the last 24 hours). After this change, 3 of the 4 allowed modifications in the rolling 24 hours are left, so the rollback is still possible.

**Current state I read** (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1):
- **Volume:** gp3, 20 GiB, Iops 3000, Throughput 125, in-use.
- **Instance:** c6i.xlarge, running, not in an Auto Scaling group. The API shows `EbsOptimized=false`, but c6i is a Nitro type, which is EBS-optimized by default.
- **Alarm:** VolumeReadBytes Sum over 60 s > 6.0e9, 3 of 3 datapoints, no alarm actions. It is currently in ALARM at about 7.87e9 bytes/min.

**Cost:** Extra gp3 throughput is billed above the free 125 MiB/s. 15 MiB/s more is roughly $0.60 per month in us-east-1 (my estimate, not checked against the price list).

**Plan check:** The plan passed the safety policy check. The first version was rejected because it had no config-backup step and no post-change checks. Both are now included.

---

## Execution plan

### Prepare
1. Save the current volume and alarm configuration. This is the rollback baseline.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 > vol-0123456789abcdef0.before.json
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region us-east-1 --alarm-names example-b-gp3-read-bytes > alarm.before.json
   ```

### Pre-validate
1. Check that no modification is in progress. Expect `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` or a `completed` record. Stop if the state is `modifying` or `optimizing`.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
   ```
2. Record the throughput before the change. Expect about 7.87e9 bytes/min, which is about 125 MiB/s.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
   ```

### Apply
1. Raise the gp3 throughput to 140 MiB/s. Only the throughput changes. This uses 1 of the 4 modifications allowed in the rolling 24 hours.
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140
   ```
   - *Risk:* a small extra cost for provisioned throughput, roughly $0.60 per month.
   - *Advisory:* the volume and instance stay online, and the new throughput applies once the state reaches `optimizing`.
2. Move the alarm threshold to 95% of the new 140 MiB/s ceiling: 140 × 1,048,576 × 60 × 0.95 = 8,367,636,480 bytes per minute. All other alarm settings stay as they are.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name example-b-gp3-read-bytes --alarm-description "example test alarm, no actions" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 --threshold 8367636480 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
   ```
   - *Advisory:* the old threshold (6.0e9, about 95.4 MiB/s) sat below the volume's own 125 MiB/s ceiling, so the alarm fired on every job run. With the new threshold, the alarm means the volume is close to saturation.

### Post-validate
1. Watch the modification go from `modifying` to `optimizing` to `completed`. Expect `TargetThroughput=140` and `TargetIops=3000`.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
   ```
2. Check the volume and alarm settings. Expect Throughput 140, Iops 3000 and Threshold 8367636480.
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput}'
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region us-east-1 --alarm-names example-b-gp3-read-bytes --query 'MetricAlarms[0].Threshold'
   ```
3. Check that throughput goes above 125 MiB/s (about 7.87e9 bytes/min before) and that `EBSByteBalance%` on `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` stays near 99%.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Minimum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
   ```
   If reads sit flat at about 140 MiB/s (about 8.81e9 bytes/min), or `EBSByteBalance%` starts falling, the job needs more than this instance's baseline allows. Plan the instance change in the follow-up below.

### Rollback
1. Set the throughput back to 125 MiB/s. Run this only after the forward change reaches `optimizing` or `completed`, because a pending modification can't be cancelled. This counts toward the 4 modifications in 24 hours.
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
   ```
2. Put the original alarm threshold back.
   ```
   aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name example-b-gp3-read-bytes --alarm-description "example test alarm, no actions" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 --threshold 6000000000 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
   ```

## Follow-up if 140 MiB/s isn't enough (plan it, not part of this change)
The job's real demand is above 125 MiB/s, but the cap hides how far above. If post-validate shows reads flat at about 140 MiB/s:
1. Schedule a maintenance window, because the instance has to stop. Stopping it drops anything on instance-local or in-memory state. The EBS data stays.
2. Change the instance type and start it again:
   ```
   aws ec2 stop-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
   aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
   aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --region us-east-1 --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --instance-type Value=c6i.2xlarge
   aws ec2 start-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
   ```
   c6i.2xlarge has a baseline of 298.0 MiB/s and 12000 IOPS. c6i.4xlarge has 596.0 MiB/s and 20000 IOPS. Either one costs more per hour than c6i.xlarge.
3. Raise the volume throughput, keeping IOPS at 3000 (well under the 750 MiB/s limit):
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 250
   ```
   Then recompute the alarm threshold as 0.95 × new MiB/s × 1,048,576 × 60.
4. To roll back: stop the instance and change it back to c6i.xlarge. Before that, the volume throughput must be back at 140 MiB/s or lower.

## Lasting fix (code/config change)
The 125 MiB/s throughput and the 6.0e9 threshold are pre-existing settings, so if this volume and alarm are managed in IaC (CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform), update the definitions to match:
- **Volume:** set `vol-0123456789abcdef0` ("example-b-gp3-throughput") to `Throughput: 140` and `Iops: 3000`, or 250 if you move to c6i.2xlarge.
  - *Done when:* the template matches the live volume, and a deploy doesn't change throughput back to 125.
  - *Done when:* the template's sizing keeps the summed demand of all volumes within the instance type's EBS baseline in MiB/s.
- **Alarm:** set `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` to `Threshold` = 0.95 × provisioned MiB/s × 1,048,576 × 60, which is 8,367,636,480 at 140 MiB/s.
  - *Done when:* the alarm stays OK during a normal job run below 95% of the provisioned throughput.
  - *Done when:* the alarm fires when reads are held at the ceiling for 3 minutes.

## Gaps
- **Real throughput demand is unknown** because the cap hides it. Whether 140 MiB/s is enough only shows up after the change.
